_about: AAASM-5714 — provenance and license manifest for execution-isolation backends.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: cargo-deny (deny.toml) is the workspace's license and
advisory gate, but it can only see crates in the cargo dependency graph. An
isolation backend that ships as a PREBUILT BINARY — bundled into a release
tarball, downloaded by the installer, or pulled into a container image —
never enters that graph, so cargo-deny never evaluates its license. Before
this manifest there was no mechanism at all covering that class of artifact.
This file is the machine-readable source of truth the gate
(scripts/check-backend-license-compliance.sh) evaluates. It records, per
backend: exact upstream name/version/source/release checksum, SPDX license,
whether AASM carries modifications, who reviewed it, and — per distribution
channel — whether AASM bundles, downloads, expects a system install, builds
from source, or does not distribute it at all.
FAIL-CLOSED BY DESIGN: `license_policy` is an ALLOWLIST with implicit deny,
mirroring deny.toml's `[licenses] allow` model. A license that is merely
unlisted is a build failure, not a warning. `known_incompatible_spdx` exists
only to turn that failure into a legible message; it is not the enforcement
mechanism, and removing an entry from it does not permit anything.
NOT LEGAL ADVICE: entries describe license identifiers and obligations as
stated in the license texts themselves. They are an engineering record for
release review, not a legal conclusion about any particular distribution.
Two allowlists, because the obligations that matter differ by whether the
consuming channel is the Apache-2.0 open-source distribution or a
proprietary (Enterprise / SaaS) one. A license in neither list is denied.
Any change to either list requires the security/licensing reviewer named
in .github/CODEOWNERS, for the same reason `[advisories] ignore` in
deny.toml must stay empty: each added entry silently widens what can ship.
_proprietary_delta: MPL-2.0 is allowed for OSS channels but NOT for proprietary ones. Reason:
MPL-2.0 §3.2 attaches per-file source-availability obligations to the
distribution of a covered work in executable form. Whether a given
proprietary bundle satisfies those obligations is a per-case decision, so
the default here is 'stop and decide', not 'allow'. Adding MPL-2.0 to
proprietary_allowed_spdx is that decision being made explicitly — which is
exactly what this ticket asks the gate to force.

known_incompatible_spdx._about: Diagnostic only — enforcement is the allowlist above. Maps a license likely to be proposed to the reason it needs an explicit decision first.
known_incompatible_spdx.AGPL-3.0-only: Network-use source-disclosure obligation (§13) reaches hosted/SaaS deployment, not only redistribution.
known_incompatible_spdx.AGPL-3.0-or-later: Network-use source-disclosure obligation (§13) reaches hosted/SaaS deployment, not only redistribution.
known_incompatible_spdx.GPL-2.0-only: Strong copyleft; combination and distribution terms need an explicit decision.
known_incompatible_spdx.GPL-3.0-only: Strong copyleft; combination and distribution terms need an explicit decision.
known_incompatible_spdx.GPL-3.0-or-later: Strong copyleft; combination and distribution terms need an explicit decision.
known_incompatible_spdx.SSPL-1.0: Not an OSI-approved license; service-source obligations reach the hosting stack.
known_incompatible_spdx.BUSL-1.1: Source-available with a use limitation and a change date, not an open-source license.
known_incompatible_spdx.Elastic-2.0: Source-available with a hosted-service use limitation, not an open-source license.

_about_packaging_paths: AAASM-5714 AC4. `packaging_paths` is the set of files IN THIS REPOSITORY
that decide what a channel actually ships. It exists so a backend's
per-channel strategy stops being an unverifiable assertion: the gate reads
these files and checks the claim against them, rather than taking the
A glob that matches no file is an error, not an empty result — a scan over
nothing would 'confirm' any claim at all. The gate also refuses a surface
made only of its own inputs (this manifest, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md, the
gate script), because a check that reads itself measures nothing.
`packaging_owner: "external-repo"` is the only way to declare an EMPTY
surface. It records that the deciding files live in another repository and
that this gate therefore cannot corroborate the claim for that channel —
an admitted blind spot rather than a silent one.

channels.notes: Assets are checksummed into SHA256SUMS and cosign keyless-signed. A bundled backend binary must get the same treatment (see docs/release/isolation-backend-licensing.md). The `Archive binaries` step in release.yml is the exact place a backend binary would enter this channel, which is why that file is the scanned surface.

Source-only channel. crates.io packages carry no prebuilt backend binary; a build.rs that downloaded one would make this a `downloaded` channel and is deliberately not permitted without a review decision.

Generator model — metadata/versions.rb IN THE TAP REPO is source of truth and formulas are regenerated from it. The formulas resolve GitHub Release assets, so this channel inherits whatever github-release ships. PARTIAL SURFACE: only the `update-homebrew-tap` job is in this repository; the formula bodies live in the tap repo, so a backend added directly to a formula there would not be seen from here — it could only reach a user through a GitHub Release asset, which release.yml does cover.

The only channel with existing SBOM coverage today (buildx `sbom: true`). An image-layer SBOM covers a backend binary baked into the image; it does NOT cover one the container downloads at runtime. The Dockerfiles are listed alongside the workflow because a binary enters an image through a Dockerfile instruction, not through the workflow that invokes buildx.

Fetches GitHub Release assets and verifies SHA256SUMS via cosign. If it is ever taught to fetch a backend from a non-AASM origin, that channel's strategy becomes `downloaded` and the license gate applies to it. scripts/install.sh is scanned too: it is the developer bootstrap rather than the published installer, but it installs host tooling and is the other script a backend could be slipped into.

Declared here so the stricter proprietary allowlist is evaluated for it. This repo cannot enforce what the enterprise repo builds; the manifest records the intended boundary and this gate fails if a backend's license is not cleared for it. Because no deciding file is in this repository, the packaging-surface corroboration below CANNOT run for this channel — that limit is declared, not worked around.

Hosted execution. Recorded because network-use obligations (e.g. AGPL §13) bite on this channel even when nothing is redistributed — the case a redistribution-only review would miss. Deciding files live in the cloud repo, so this channel is not corroborable from here either.

review.capability_evidence: ci.yml job `isolation-backend-linux` installs exactly this artifact (digest verified by `sha256sum -c` in the job), then runs `aa-isolation-sandlock`'s confinement suite, which measures each claimed capability against observed behaviour with a control for every scenario: a forbidden write leaves an existing file byte-for-byte unchanged and creates nothing (pre-effect), a forbidden read returns no bytes, a connection to an unpermitted loopback destination never reaches a listener this repository owns, a process ceiling of one stops a grandchild from existing, and a descendant re-invoking the mechanism with a wider grant is still denied while the identical command outside the boundary succeeds. `.ci/test-evidence-summary.sh --require-evidence` fails the job if every scenario declined, so a green lane cannot mean an unmeasured one. A version bump must re-run that lane: the capability reports in `aa-isolation-sandlock/src/capability.rs` are gated on the live probe, so a version that stops denying reports itself as unable to prevent rather than passing on the strength of this record.

_about: The executable name(s) AASM would have to name somewhere in its
packaging code in order to ship this backend. The gate greps every
channel's `packaging_paths` for these strings and requires the
result to agree with `channels` below: a backend claiming
non-distribution everywhere must appear NOWHERE in the packaging
surface, and a backend claiming `bundled`/`downloaded`/`source`
must appear SOMEWHERE in the surface of a channel it claims.
Matching is a case-insensitive substring, deliberately over-broad. A
false positive is a loud failure someone reads and resolves; a false
negative is the silent hole this whole file exists to close.
Note what this does NOT cover: ci.yml installs this exact binary in
the `isolation-backend-linux` job, and that is correct — a CI test
lane is not a distribution channel, so ci.yml is in no channel's
packaging surface and the install there does not trip this probe.

notes: MEASURED, NOT QUOTED. Every field above was taken from the artifact:
the digest was computed locally with `shasum -a 256` over the downloaded
tarball and matches the digest GitHub publishes for that release asset;
the SPDX identifier was read from the LICENSE file at tag v0.8.6.
AASM DISTRIBUTES NOTHING. The backend is an external executable the
operator installs, so no channel is `bundled`, `downloaded` or `source`
and none is license-gated by this file. `crates-io` is
`not-distributed` rather than `system` for a different reason: the
consuming crate `aa-isolation-sandlock` carries `publish = false`, so
nothing on that channel could use the backend even if it were present.
The digest is not decoration. `ci.yml`'s `isolation-backend-linux` job
pins this exact version and verifies this exact digest before it
measures anything, so a drifted upstream artifact fails CI instead of
silently changing what was measured. Bumping `version` without bumping
`release_sha256` breaks that job.
WHAT THIS ROW DOES NOT SAY: it records provenance, not capability. What
the backend can actually enforce is measured per host at run time and
reported through `aa-isolation`'s capability contract; the mechanism's
own feature documentation is not used as an AASM claim anywhere.

backends.upstream_name: Linux kernel, built via linuxkit's kernel build tooling
backends.version: kernel.org 6.6.71, linuxkit commit 2308529, 3 Kconfig patches (Landlock, LSM list, virtio/vsock/vhost)

review.capability_evidence: `aa_isolation_macos_vm::probe::measure` boots a real guest running exactly this kernel and measures FilesystemRead/FilesystemWrite as a control/test pair (a granted path readable/writable, an ungranted path denied, never asserted from the kernel's own documentation) — see `aa-isolation-macos-vm/src/probe.rs` and the real-hardware evidence in `aa-isolation-macos-vm/tests/real_hardware.rs::discover_measures_real_capability_rows`. The syscall-filter domain is reported `Unsupported` truthfully (`capability::syscall_unsupported`) rather than claimed, since `aa_isolation_native`'s x86_64-only filter has no arm64 counterpart. A kernel swap invalidates this row: `discover()`'s probe re-measures on every backend construction, so a kernel that regresses a capability reports itself unable rather than passing on the strength of this record.

notes: AASM DISTRIBUTES NOTHING (AAASM-5840). This is a large, gitignored,
hand-built dev artifact (`aa-isolation-macos-vm/src/vmm.rs::VmConfig`'s
own docs) the operator supplies via `AA_ISOLATION_MACOS_VM_KERNEL` — no
channel is `bundled`, `downloaded` or `source`, so `GPL-2.0-only` is not
added to either `license_policy` allowlist: this row is not gated by
them (see `GATED_STRATEGIES` in the gate script), and adding a license
to an allowlist is a security/licensing-reviewer decision (CODEOWNERS),
not one this row should make preemptively. The day AAASM-5840 ships
this artifact through any channel, that channel's strategy changes to
`bundled`/`downloaded`/`source` and the gate starts failing here until
a human adds `GPL-2.0-only` to the relevant allowlist and this row
carries a real notice-of-modification path a recipient can actually
reach — the fail-closed behavior this file exists to guarantee.
`distribution_probe.binary_names` deliberately does not use the bare
words `kernel` or `Image`: `kernel` hits `scripts/install-cli.sh` and
`Image` hits roughly two dozen Dockerfiles, both false positives that
would permanently trip this row's own check. `images-landlock-kernel`
is the exact path fragment a packaging step would have to name to ship
this specific artifact, and does not appear anywhere in the current
packaging surface today.
MODIFIED: three Kconfig changes on top of linuxkit's own published
6.6.x/config-aarch64 (CONFIG_SECURITY_LANDLOCK, the active LSM list,
and virtio/vsock/vhost flipped built-in) — see the notice_path script
for the exact patch and why each line is there. The underlying kernel
source itself is unmodified upstream kernel.org 6.6.71, fetched and
GPG/SHA256-verified by linuxkit's own build tooling.

backends.version: busybox:musl, Docker Hub image digest sha256:32b5cdad7cce41dfd53d0ae06baebcf8357a147ee7694dc706911c373bc30c37 (upstream does not tag a bare busybox release version for this image; the pinned image digest is the actual provenance anchor `fetch-busybox.sh` verifies against)

review.capability_evidence: Same real-guest measurement as `macos-vm-guest-kernel` above: `busybox` is the program every launch in `aa-isolation-macos-vm/src/probe.rs` and `aa-isolation-macos-vm/tests/real_hardware.rs` actually executes inside the guest to produce the FilesystemRead/FilesystemWrite control/test pairs. It provides the guest's `sh`/`cat`/`printf` as a single static-PIE binary with no dynamic-linker dependency (see `fetch-busybox.sh`'s own docs), which is why it is the confined workload rather than a stand-in for one.

notes: AASM DISTRIBUTES NOTHING (AAASM-5840) — same reasoning as
`macos-vm-guest-kernel` above: no channel is gated, `GPL-2.0-only` is
deliberately not added to either allowlist, and the day this changes
the gate fails closed until a human reviewer decides. The digest is
extracted byte-for-byte from the pinned Docker image (`fetch-busybox.sh`)
with no build step of AASM's own, hence `modifications.modified: false`.
`guest-rootfs.img` is listed alongside `busybox-aarch64` in
`distribution_probe.binary_names` because it is the assembled ext4 image
a packaging step would actually have to name to ship this backend's
guest content — it also carries first-party `aa-isolation-launch` and
`guest-init` (Apache-2.0, not third-party; see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).
Its own digest is a build artifact, not upstream provenance, so it is
not recorded as this row's `release_sha256`.
